title: Hally's
status: Existing V2: preserve and reconcile separately
description: A neighbourhood café in Parsons Green, reimagined around a single idea: a tangle of moments.
metadata: Client Hally's Scope Rebrand, Website, Menu, Illustration Based Parsons Green, London Relationship 10+ years

editorialSequence.text: The Challenge Hally's has been serving its Parsons Green neighbourhood for over a decade — a cosy, welcoming café that had never quite had branding to match. Anna, the owner, wanted a fresh, elegant identity that still felt like the place regulars already loved: engaging, energetic, unmistakably itself.
Brand Story A Tangle of Moments

The Approach The idea we landed on was a tangle of moments — every café is a quiet stage where lives briefly cross: friends meet, strangers exchange a glance, a neighbour pauses for a break, then moves on. We built a visual system around that convergence: a single wandering line, drawn loose and looping like light painting, threading through the illustrations, packaging, menus, and site. Lora, a modern serif with roots in calligraphy, gave the looseness of the hand-drawn line something to push against — refinement meeting casualness.
+ Wandering Paths + Light Painting = A Tangle of Moments

“I have worked with Jason for over 10 years now; the latest project was the recent rebrand of my neighbourhood café, Hally’s. The visual narrative that he landed on was perfect, unique, tasteful and bold, making us stand out. […] across all of our channels and collateral, and which completely captured the essence of Hally’s. Jason’s concept extended perfectly to the website, menu and beyond. He is a brilliant illustrator too.”
The Illustrations A hand-drawn set built alongside the wandering line — cocktails, glassware, and small in-jokes that show up across the menu, packaging, and site.
Colours A palette built to feel as vibrant and easygoing as the café itself — from the soft warmth of Flat White to the grounding calm of Charcoal.

Typography — Lora The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog AaBbCcDdEeFfGgHhIiJjKkLlMmNnOoPpQqRrSsTtUuVvWwXxYyZz 0123456789 "Lora offers a grounded counterbalance — a modern serif with roots in calligraphy, combining classic elegance with a contemporary rhythm." Aa

The Outcome The new identity now carries Hally's across every touchpoint — website, menus, tote bags, packaging, seasonal posters — all speaking the same wandering-line language. A decade into the relationship, it's a brand that finally looks and feels like the café people already loved.
Client Anna Halliday, Founder, Hally's

title: Sussex
description: A wordmark built from a county flag, for the Gladwin Brothers' flagship wine bar and restaurant.
metadata: Client Sussex, Local & Wild Scope Logo, Brand System, Typography Based London Concept Six Birds, One Stone

editorialSequence.text: The Challenge Sussex needed to feel distinct from the Gladwin Brothers' six other London restaurants — refined, intentional, and rooted in a specific place, not just another wine bar.
Brand Story Six Birds, One Stone

The Approach The solution came from a detail most people never notice: Sussex is the only English county whose flag carries six golden martlets in a triangular formation. Rather than design a conventional logo, we let the name itself take that shape — SUSSEX set across three lines in a triangular grid mirroring the flag, the X anchoring the composition like a keystone. The system flexes: six coffee beans for takeaway, six wine droplets for the wine list, six wildflowers for seasonal menus — same rhythm, shifting tone.
+ Wine Grapes + The Sussex Flag + Typewriter Type = The Wordmark

The System, Flexing The same grid flexes across contexts: six martlets for the core mark, six coffee beans for takeaway, six wine droplets for the wine list, six wildflowers for seasonal menus. Same rhythm, shifting tone.
"Now, with six thriving restaurants across London, Jason's unparalleled creativity and vision have been essential at every turn."

Posters Each event poster subtly references the six martlets of the Sussex flag through a triangular arrangement — six small plates for Tapas Night, six glass silhouettes for Cocktail Hour, six abstract forms for the gallery event. Quiet continuity across the campaign, with room to vary.
Colours A palette built around the region itself — the deep tonal qualities of the South Downs, balanced against an unexpected breath of spring.

Typography — Prestige Elite The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog AaBbCcDdEeFfGgHhIiJjKkLlMmNnOoPpQqRrSsTtUuVvWwXxYyZz 0123456789 "A monospaced typewriter font designed by Howard Kettler in 1953 — its evenly spaced, mechanical rhythm adds structure and a sense of deliberation, a nod to literary tradition and a reminder of craft." Aa

The Menu Presented like a clothbound book — a small gesture that hints at story, permanence, and care. Inside, minimal and deliberate, letting the food take the lead. Business cards and coasters follow the same restrained language.

The Outcome The triangular system now runs across menus, signage, business cards, and event posters — a mark that rewards curiosity, instantly legible to locals and layered with meaning for everyone else.
Client Richard Gladwin, CEO, Local & Wild

title: The Fat Badger
description: A farmer walks into a bar — a restaurant and farm shop in one, for the Gladwin Brothers' seventh London location.
A Farmer Walks Into a Bar…
metadata: Client The Fat Badger, Local & Wild Scope Logo, Brand Development, Bag Design Based London Concept A Farmer Walks Into a Bar…

editorialSequence.text: The Challenge The Gladwin Brothers wanted a visual identity that could hold two ideas at once: a fine-dining restaurant and a fresh, seasonal grocer, sharing one roof. It needed to resonate with their existing clientele while pulling in a new one entirely.
Brand Story A Farmer Walks Into a Bar…

The Approach The moodboard leaned into handpainted signage — the emphasis on typography and the craft of its execution. We loved the texture of one weathered old sign in particular, the way age had worn into the letterforms, and borrowed that as inspiration for texture within our own type. The arcs in the composition, both structural and decorative, came from the same source.
+ Handpainted Signage + Farm-to-Fork Ethos = The Fat Badger
"Since launching our first restaurant, The Shed, in 2012, we've had the privilege of collaborating with Jason de Villiers. His innovative input is a game-changer for any new business."

Logo Development A flexible visual system for all applications — the full lockup, a solid reversal, a standalone wordmark, and the badger-head mark on its own, each one built to hold up at any size, from a farm shop sign to a jar label.

Colours Two shades that reflect the farm-to-fork ethos while drawing from nature: Camo Green captures the earthy tones of fresh produce and the outdoors, while Lichen evokes the soft, mossy greens found growing wild.

Typography — TT Norms & Copperplate Extended The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog AaBbCcDdEeFfGgHhIiJjKkLlMmNnOoPpQqRrSsTtUuVvWwXxYyZz 0123456789 "TT Norms offers a clean, modern aesthetic for body copy; the extended letterforms and sharp serifs of Copperplate Extended bring refinement and authority to the headline. Together, a balance between heritage and modernity." Aa

Poster & Tote Bag "Lettuce, Turnip the Beet" — a headline that blends fresh produce with a clever pun, echoing the restaurant's playful blend of natural ingredients and lively atmosphere. The tote bag carries the same spirit: a pesto recipe on one side, the ingredients and tools to make it on the other.

The Outcome A flexible visual system now runs across signage, bags, and collateral — one identity, doing double duty as both restaurant and grocer, without ever feeling like two brands wearing one badge.
Client Richard Gladwin, CEO, Local & Wild

title: Wright Architects
description: A wordmark built on a single precise cut — an identity as considered as the practice it belongs to.
metadata: Client Wright Architects Scope Logo, Signage, Stationery Based Cape Town Concept Surgical Precision

editorialSequence.text: The Challenge Wright Architects needed a mark that could sit on a waterfront office front, a business card, and a set of drawings alike, and read as exactly what the practice is: precise, considered, unshowy. Nothing about it could look decorative — every line had to earn its place. I worked alongside creative director Warren van Rensburg , who helped shape the brand's positioning, strategy, and creative direction.
Brand Story Surgical Precision

The Approach The whole identity turns on a single decision: every terminal in the wordmark is cut at exactly 17.5°, the same angle, repeated without exception. Set it against a straight edge and the cut all but disappears — subtle enough that most people will never consciously clock it. Soften those terminals back to a plain 90°, though, and the mark goes flat: it loses the quiet tension that makes it read as drawn, not typed. That's "surgical precision" in one detail — a cut small enough to go unnoticed, essential enough to hold the whole structure together. The kind of exactness a good architect works in without ever pointing at it.

The Outcome The same 17.5° geometry carries the identity across the whole practice — signage, business cards, letterhead — without a single additional flourish. A mark built on restraint, for a practice that trades on the same.
Client Greg Wright, Director, Wright Architects

title: Hām
description: An affordable fine dining restaurant in West Hampstead, where fine dining is made accessible to everyone.
metadata: Client Hām Scope Logo, Brand Identity, Menu Design Based West Hampstead, London Concept Art Deco-dence

editorialSequence.text: The Challenge Hām needed a logo that captured its heart: elegant and distinctive, with bold elements that still feel familiar. Working closely with co-founder Rose Tuckey, the visual identity had to match the restaurant's Art Deco interior and its stylish, vintage ambience.
Brand Story Art Deco-dence

The Approach "Hām" is Old English for "home" — a fitting anchor for a neighbourhood restaurant that wanted to feel like somewhere you could always come back to. That idea, paired with the geometry and glamour of the Art Deco movement, became the visual language: bold, symmetrical, warmly lit.
+ Art Deco + Hām Brand = Home
Colours A palette pulled straight from the room — the warmth of aged brass, the cool weight of stone, the quiet green of the booths.
The Outcome The identity now runs through the menu, signage, and social presence — bold and symmetrical where the room is bold and symmetrical, warm where the room is warm.
Client Rose Tuckey, Co-Founder, Hām

title: Scott USA
description: A global art collaboration, passed from artist to artist across continents — one canvas, one long story.
metadata: Client Scott USA Scope Illustration, Packaging Design Based South Africa Concept Global Collaboration

editorialSequence.text: The Brief Scott USA had a wild idea for their snowboarding products: a global art collaboration that felt like a creative chain letter, passing one canvas from artist to artist across continents, each adding their own piece to the story.

The Approach When the canvas reached South Africa, I was the third artist to contribute — the only one chosen from the entire African continent, which meant a great deal. I painted a fisherman, fitting for a canvas that had already crossed an ocean with a long journey still ahead. At the time I went by "Further," a nod to Ken Kesey and the Merry Pranksters' bus, worked into the piece as both signature and a marker of the distance between each artist involved. That piece became the hero image on the final packaging and t-shirt design.
"Working with Jason is an excellent experience. He is a talented, hard-working professional that is passionate about his craft."
The Outcome A surreal, proud moment: a painting born from a single South African contribution to a global chain, ending up as the face of the product itself.
Client Nowel Pawliw, Art Director, Scott USA

title: G Adventures
description: A custom illustration and icon system for a travel company running over 700 itineraries in more than 100 countries.
metadata: Client G Adventures Scope Illustration, Iconography Based International Concept Website Illustrations

editorialSequence.text: The Brief G Adventures specializes in guided tours for small groups, tailoring travel packages to each traveler's preferences — they even collaborate with National Geographic on some trips. To stand out in a market crowded with photography, we decided to lead with custom illustration instead.
Brand Story A World in Icons

The Approach Working with G Adventures' upper management, we developed a unique graphic style built to scale across the site — header postcards for each region of the world, and a full icon set covering everything from booking status to trip type. Same linework, same warmth, wherever a traveler lands on the site.
Header Postcards A postcard illustration for every region G Adventures operates in — each one distinct, all of them clearly part of the same family.
The Icon Set A full library covering booking status, trip type, and traveler preference — small enough to sit next to a line of copy, distinctive enough to carry the brand on their own.

"Illustrations played an important part of the project and we were thrilled with the results. Jason was collaborative, and went above and beyond with a fresh perspective that made the results even better."
Trees for Life The same illustration language extended to G Adventures' sustainability initiatives — giving the environmental side of the business the same warmth as the trip-planning side.

The Outcome A cohesive illustration system now carries G Adventures across the entire site — recognisable at a glance, warm at every touchpoint, built to grow as new destinations and features are added.
Client Greg Cormier, VP Digital & E-Commerce, G Adventures

editorialSequence.text: About I Art Joburg is a street art event held in South Africa, where local and international artists come together to create large-scale murals in the often-overlooked streets of Johannesburg — injecting a wave of positivity as neglected buildings receive vibrant facelifts.

The Backstory Working alongside /ANDPEOPLE, the concept was to upcycle a commonplace box by laser-engraving a South African-inspired pattern onto its exterior. The cardboard stands in for the raw material of the buildings themselves — with one simple creative action, something new is born. Designer and Art Director Kim Terri Smith curated everything inside the box, along with the booklet and broadsheet design.

title: Selected Brandmarks
description: Behind every simple logo is a not-so-simple idea. A look behind the curtain at how these marks came to life.
metadata: Client Selected Studio Work Scope Logo / Wordmark, Concept Breakdown Based International Concept A Reduction of a Reduction

editorialSequence.text: About the Process The marks here are rooted in strategy, story, and reduction — a balance between clarity and meaning. Each logo begins as a thought experiment: how do you express the soul of a brand using as little as possible? The answer often lives in dualities — function and feeling, concept and form.
Brand Story Start With Meaning

The Backstory Every logo starts with listening — getting close to a brand's personality, its ambitions, the people behind it. From there it's distillation: references, sketches, metaphors, patterns that feel both familiar and surprising. More often than not, the solution arrives when two distinct ideas lock together. That's where the spark is. That's where the logo begins.

Tortuga Loca — Mexican Radiance For this bold, vibrant Mexican kitchen, the logo brings together symbolism from faith and folklore. A sharp monogram "T" radiates outward from a hexagonal frame — the hexagon a nod to a tortoise-shell plate, the radiant lines borrowed from the iconography of Our Lady of Guadalupe. Grounded and glowing, at once.
+ Our Lady of Guadalupe + Tortoise Shell = Tortuga Loca

Wilma — Caring First Wilma supports people through the challenging days after losing a loved one, making estate transfers clearer and easier. Rounded letterforms and a small heart hidden in the "m" convey warmth — modern, comforting, and quietly optimistic, unlike the neutral tones common in the industry.

Good Luck — Bottled Goodness This bottled citrus brand brings together grapefruit, blood orange, and lime. The wordmark divides into eight even segments — the natural geometry of citrus cut crosswise, and the brand's core values: simple, and full of character.

Outlier Health — Eternal Balance Balance sits at the heart of Outlier Medicine, a practice rooted in Eastern tradition. The logo draws from the yin-yang symbol, reinterpreted within a single letter — the "O" — transforming the brand's initial into a quiet symbol of equilibrium.
Some logos tell you everything in a glance.

The Shed — Farm to Fork For The Shed, a farm-to-fork restaurant, the usual knife and fork symbol became a gardener's fork and trowel — tools of the soil instead of the kitchen. A quiet visual shift that reframes the whole experience: great food starts in the ground.
The Outcome Five brands, five different problems — the same process underneath each one: listen first, reduce until only the idea is left, then shape it into a mark that feels inevitable.
